description: We are a creative team from Rangpur, Bangladesh, . For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we aim to bring the “Abandoned but Not Forgotten” challenge to life through research and engaging digital experiences. We welcome teammates skilled in coding, web development,  UI/UX, data visualization, or scientific research. Let’s learn, collaborate, and create something meaningful together!
summary:
Astro Legacy is a phone-first, interactive story web app that makes hard space-hardware data simple for school-age space enthusiasts.

Since the 1960s, NASA has left hardware on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space: rovers and instruments that finished their missions, and probes still traveling. Most young people have never heard their stories. Astro Legacy tells them.

VIMO, our interactive guide, takes users on one story from Earth to deep space and back. A quick 3D tour and 3D map show every machine at its real location and time. Three lobbies (Moon, Mars, deep space) organize 57 machines, each explained through conversation, short videos, cards and games, with its purpose, its current status and the science it made possible. Archie, our built-in AI assistant, opens more NASA data, and users can step inside the hardware to experience how missions worked. A sorting game, quiz and shareable certificate check what was learned. Every fact links to its NASA source.

It is free, works in English and Bangla, and has a lite mode for everyday devices. In classrooms and homes, it could inspire the kids who build our next machines.
details:
What it does

Astro Legacy is a phone-first, interactive story web app about the hardware NASA has left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space since the 1960s. Our guide VIMO takes users on one seamless story from Earth to deep space and back. A quick 3D tour and an interactive 3D map show every machine at its real location and time. Three lobbies (Moon, Mars, deep space) organize 57 machines: rovers and instruments that finished their missions, landers, descent stages, and probes still traveling. For each one, users learn what it was for, whether it still works, and the science it made possible.

How it works

Each stop follows one rhythm: VIMO and the machine talk with the user, a short video explains the hard idea through a story, a card gives the key fact with its NASA source, and a "Try it" game lets users learn by doing (for example, bouncing a laser off the Apollo 11 mirror). Archie, our built-in AI assistant, opens more NASA data and answers questions. Users can step inside the hardware to face real mission problems, such as driving a rover with the real Earth-Mars signal delay. A sorting game, quiz, logbook and shareable certificate check and reward learning.

Benefits and intended impact

Hard space data becomes a story school-age kids can follow, feel and remember. It is free, needs no sign-up, works in English and Bangla, and has a lite mode for everyday phones, so students without labs or museums can explore real NASA science. In classrooms and homes, it could inspire the kids who build our next machines.

Why it is creative

The machines become characters with their own stories, guided by an original mascot. Learning happens through doing and through real mission decisions, not memorizing. Every fact links to its NASA source.

Tools and technology

React, TypeScript and Vite; three.js (React Three Fiber) for real-time 3D; GSAP for animation; Blender for preparing NASA 3D models; Gemini API for the Archie assistant; ElevenLabs for voice and sound; GitHub and Netlify for code and hosting.

NASA data used

NASA 3D Resources models, NASA Image and Video Library, Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter imagery, CGI Moon Kit, NASA Mars maps, NSSDCA mission records and NASA mission pages.

What our team considered

Accuracy first: anything we could not confirm on a NASA page was removed. Kid safety and wellbeing: no tracking, no scary content, captions always on. Performance on low-cost phones. No NASA logos or branding.
